title: Verification effort: Better AI may not raise output
desc: Shows theoretically that skill-dependent checking can offset stronger assistance and produce divergent, but not inevitable, long-run skill effects.

kps.k: Better AI need not raise productivity when people adjust their effort.
kps.d: Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes contributes conditional mathematical theory, not empirical findings about lawyers or workplaces. Its baseline model assumes concave production and linear effort costs: greater human skill, AI proficiency or AI reliability weakly reduces utility-maximizing effort by lowering its marginal return. In a capped-linear example, effort reductions can make productivity decline as AI proficiency rises. This challenges an automatic link between better tools and better output, but does not establish that AI generally harms productivity; the result differs when human effort has already reached zero.

kps.k: Skill-dependent verification can make more-skilled people exert more effort over particular skill ranges.
kps.d: The model identifies two mechanisms through which checking AI output changes effort incentives. When reliability falls below one-half, changing signal probabilities can place more weight on the higher-effort response to a low-quality signal. Separately, more-skilled verification can reduce perceived AI usefulness enough to trigger a sharp effort increase after a low-quality signal. These reversals require specific assumptions about production, effort costs, verification accuracy and parameter thresholds; verification or AI assistance alone does not guarantee them.

kps.k: Divergent long-run skill outcomes are possible, not inevitable.
kps.d: Assuming effort increases skill advancement, the paper proves that effort declining with skill produces a single-peaked steady-state skill distribution across all admissible skill-state sets and positive decay rates. Non-monotonic effort instead permits multiple peaks for suitably chosen skill states and decay rates. This is an existence result, not a prediction that AI will polarize the workforce. The distinction matters because the long-run outcome depends on both effort incentives and the assumed process of skill accumulation and decay.

kps.k: The decisive qualification concerns how verification ability varies with skill, rather than AI capability alone.
kps.d: Under any concave production function and linear effort costs, constant verification accuracy of at least one-half makes expected effort weakly decrease with skill and reliability. With advancement increasing in effort, the long-run skill distribution then remains single-peaked. The supplied material contains no competing empirical account; its central tension lies between conditional model regimes. A practical implication is to examine human effort responses, checking ability and learning alongside AI performance when assessing deployment, rather than infer workforce effects from capability gains alone. The paper does not test which training or deployment policies work.

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research source supports the cluster’s principal proposition through a conditional mathematical model rather than empirical evidence about legal practice or workplaces. It shows that increasing AI proficiency, reliability, or human skill can reduce utility-maximizing effort, so capability improvements do not automatically translate into higher realised productivity. It also supports the proposition’s qualified long-run claim: when verification accuracy varies with skill, effort can become non-monotonic and a multimodal skill distribution can exist. The material’s principal internal variation is between model regimes, not disagreement among researchers: non-monotonic effort requires specific production, cost, verification, and threshold assumptions, while constant verification accuracy produces declining effort and a unimodal skill distribution. Thus the source supports divergent skill effects as a possibility, not an inevitable forecast. Because the curated evidence contains one theoretical source, this position should not be treated as representative of academia and research generally.

elens.an: The 2026 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition through conditional mathematical theory rather than empirical evidence about workplaces or legal practice. It models how improvements in AI proficiency or reliability can reduce utility-maximizing human effort, so stronger assistance need not translate into higher realized productivity. It also supports the proposition’s emphasis on verification: when checking accuracy varies with skill, effort can become non-monotonic and can permit a multimodal long-run skill distribution. Material variation lies across model regimes, not competing sources. These effects require specified production, cost, reliability and verification conditions; without the relevant condition, effort declines with skill, and constant verification accuracy yields a unimodal skill distribution. The source therefore presents divergent skill outcomes as possible rather than inevitable. Because the curated evidence for this period contains one theoretical source, it establishes a coherent mechanism and qualifications but not the mechanism’s empirical prevalence or practical magnitude.
